speaker_role: current admissions officer (Gabe Brown, Associate Director of Admission at the University of Notre Dame, 17 years in the office)
commercial_incentive: none evident; public high school district information session
key_insights: Defines 'selective' as admitting fewer than roughly a third of applicants, noting this applies to a minority of US colleges; roughly two-thirds of US colleges admit more than half of applicants
Describes a feedback loop where growing, unpredictable applicant pools push students to apply to more schools for options, which further inflates pools and selectivity
At test-optional Notre Dame, whether to submit a score is left fully to the student's discretion, and an application can be equally competitive either way
Academic evaluation weighs rigor relative to what's actually offered at the student's specific high school, grade trends over time, and whether transcript strength aligns with an intended major
Extracurricular evaluation is agnostic between many shallow activities versus deep commitment to a few, and explicitly counts part-time jobs and family caregiving as legitimate activities
Some admissions criteria reflect purely institutional needs (specific majors, instruments, class-gender balance) that are entirely outside an applicant's control
specific_numbers_or_facts: Selective defined as admitting fewer than roughly one-third of applicants (Gabe Brown)
Roughly two-thirds of US colleges admit more than half of their applicants (Gabe Brown)
notable_or_distinctive: a sitting Notre Dame admissions officer directly confirms that test-optional truly means either submission path yields an equally competitive file, and explicitly states jobs/family caregiving count as legitimate extracurricular time
reliability_notes: presenter repeatedly caveats that some policies (e.g., interview requirements) are school/major-specific and he cannot speak for other institutions; content is a credible first-person account from a named officer with minimal transcription issues
